title: No. 52 — The House of Representatives (Madison)
paragraphs: The first thing to examine about this part of the government concerns the qualifications of voters and elected officials. The qualifications of voters will be the same as those for voters in the most numerous branch of the State legislatures. The definition of the right to vote is rightly seen as a fundamental article of republican government. The convention therefore had to define and establish this right in the Constitution. Leaving it open for occasional regulation by Congress would have been improper, for the reason just given. Submitting it to the discretion of State legislatures would have been improper for the same reason. It would also have made too dependent on State governments that branch of the federal government which ought to depend on the people alone. Reducing the different qualifications in the different States to one uniform rule would probably have been as unsatisfactory to some States as it would have been difficult for the convention. The provision the convention made therefore appears to be the best option available. It must satisfy every State, because it conforms to the standard already established, or which may be established, by the State itself. It will be safe for the United States, because, being fixed by the State constitutions, it cannot be altered by the State governments. There is no fear that the people of the States will alter this part of their constitutions in a way that abridges the rights guaranteed to them by the federal Constitution.

The qualifications for elected representatives are less carefully defined by the State constitutions and are also more open to uniform treatment. The convention therefore properly considered and regulated them. A representative of the United States must be at least twenty-five years old. He must have been a citizen of the United States for seven years. At the time of his election, he must live in the State he is to represent. And during his service, he must hold no other office under the United States. Under these reasonable limits, the door to this part of the federal government is open to merit of every kind. Native or naturalized, young or old, rich or poor, of any religious faith — all may serve.

The term for which representatives will be elected is the second matter to consider about this branch. To decide whether this article is sound, two questions must be examined. First, will biennial elections be safe in this case? Second, are they necessary or useful?

First. Liberty requires that the government in general share a common interest with the people. It is especially essential that the branch under consideration depend immediately on the people and feel close sympathy with them. Frequent elections are unquestionably the only policy by which this dependence and sympathy can be effectively secured. But what specific frequency is absolutely necessary cannot be calculated precisely. It must depend on a variety of related circumstances. Let us consult experience, the guide that should always be followed when it can be found.

The system of representation, as a substitute for the citizens meeting in person, was at most very imperfectly known to ancient politics. Only in modern times can we expect to find instructive examples. And even here, to avoid research that is too vague and scattered, we should confine ourselves to the few examples best known and most analogous to our case. The first to consider is the House of Commons in Great Britain. The history of this branch of the English Constitution before Magna Carta is too obscure to teach us much. Even its very existence has been disputed by political historians. The earliest later records show that parliaments were to MEET only every year, not that they were to be ELECTED every year. And even these annual sessions were left so much to the king's discretion that, under various pretexts, royal ambition often contrived very long and dangerous gaps between them. To remedy this grievance, a statute in the reign of Charles II provided that the gaps should not extend beyond three years. When William III came to the throne and a revolution took place, the subject was taken up again more seriously. It was declared a fundamental right of the people that parliaments ought to be held FREQUENTLY. By another statute passed a few years later in the same reign, the term "frequently," which had referred to the three-year period set under Charles II, was given a precise meaning. It was expressly enacted that a new parliament must be called within three years after the previous one ended. The last change, from three to seven years, was introduced early in the present century, during alarm over the Hanoverian succession. From these facts it appears that the greatest frequency of elections deemed necessary in that kingdom for binding representatives to their constituents does not exceed every three years. And if we judge from the degree of liberty retained even under seven-year elections, with all the other flaws in the parliamentary constitution, we cannot doubt this. A reduction from seven to three years, with the other necessary reforms, would extend the people's influence over their representatives enough to satisfy us. Biennial elections under the federal system cannot possibly threaten the necessary dependence of the House of Representatives on their constituents.

Elections in Ireland, until recently, were regulated entirely by the discretion of the crown. They were seldom repeated except when a new monarch came to the throne, or some other contingent event occurred. The parliament that began with George II continued throughout his whole reign, a period of about thirty-five years. The only dependence the representatives had on the people consisted in the people's right to fill occasional vacancies by electing new members, and in the chance of some event producing a general new election. The Irish parliament's ability to defend the rights of its constituents, even where the will to do so existed, was severely limited by the crown's control over the subjects of their deliberation. Recently, if I am not mistaken, these restraints have been broken. Eight-year parliaments have also been established. What effect this partial reform may produce must be left to further experience. The example of Ireland, viewed this way, sheds little light on our subject. As far as we can draw any conclusion from it, it must be this. If the people of that country have been able to retain any liberty at all under such disadvantages, biennial elections would secure them every degree of liberty that depends on a proper connection between representatives and the people.

Let us bring our inquiry closer to home. The example of these States, when they were British colonies, deserves particular attention. It is so well known that little needs to be said. The principle of representation, in at least one branch of the legislature, was established in all of them. But the periods of election varied. They ranged from one to seven years. Do we have any reason to infer, from the spirit and conduct of the representatives of the people before the Revolution, that biennial elections would have been dangerous to the public liberties? The spirit displayed everywhere at the start of the struggle, which overcame the obstacles to independence, is the best proof that a sufficient measure of liberty had been enjoyed everywhere. It inspired both a sense of liberty's worth and a zeal for its proper extension. This is true as much of the colonies whose elections were least frequent as of those whose elections were most frequent. Virginia was the colony that stood first in resisting the parliamentary usurpations of Great Britain. It was also the first to embrace, by public act, the resolution of independence. Yet in Virginia, if I have not been misinformed, elections under the former government were every seven years. I cite this example not as proof of any peculiar merit, since the priority in those instances was probably accidental. Still less do I cite it as showing any advantage in SEVEN-YEAR elections. Compared with greater frequency they are unacceptable. I cite it merely as proof, and a very substantial proof, that the liberties of the people can be in no danger from BIENNIAL elections.

The conclusion drawn from these examples will be considerably strengthened by recalling three points. First, the federal legislature will possess only part of that supreme legislative authority which is fully vested in the British Parliament, and which, with a few exceptions, was exercised by the colonial assemblies and the Irish legislature. It is a well-founded maxim that, where no other circumstances affect the case, the greater the power, the shorter its duration ought to be. Conversely, the smaller the power, the more safely its duration may be extended. Second, it has been shown elsewhere that the federal legislature will be restrained not only by its dependence on the people, as other legislative bodies are, but it will also be watched and controlled by the several State legislatures, which other legislative bodies are not. Third, no comparison can be made between the means available to the more permanent branches of the federal government for seducing the House of Representatives from its duty to the people, if they should be inclined to do so, and the means of influence over the popular branch possessed by the other branches of government cited above. With less power to abuse, the federal representatives can be less tempted on one side, and will be doubly watched on the other.
